These exercises go with the Week 5 lecture. Part A checks your understanding of the
ideas. Parts B–E are problems to work through, in the same order as the lecture: the
seven questions, the bicycle case, estimands, and the target trial. Part F is the main
assignment from the last slide: a critique memo, plus a check on your own project.
Part G is an optional R challenge.

A few ground rules:

- **Show your work.** A correct answer with no reasoning is worth less than a wrong
  answer with clear reasoning. For many of these questions, drawing a small DAG is the
  easiest way to think.
- **Write in plain language.** If you can't explain it to a friend who missed the
  lecture, you haven't finished understanding it yet.
- **There is often more than one good answer.** This week is about judgement. Say what
  you assume, and why.
- Problems marked ★ are harder. Give them a real try, but don't get stuck on them.

All the studies, programs, and numbers in this homework are **made up for practice**,
unless the question says it comes from the lecture slides.

# Part A: Concepts

**A1.** Write the seven questions to ask of any finding, from memory if you can. Next to
each one, write the week of the course it comes from (Week 1, 2, 3 or 4). Which one or
two are new this week?

**A2.** Is each sentence a **descriptive**, **predictive**, or **causal** claim? Underline
any causal verbs (words like *boosts, drives, leads to, protects against*).

a. "In our survey of 500 households in Dhading, 1 in 4 received money from a family
   member working abroad."
b. "Remittances drive higher school enrollment in the hills."
c. "Given the rain so far this monsoon, the river will probably flood in August."
d. "Students who use the school library more get better grades."
e. "Using the school library boosts grades."

Pick one causal claim. Rewrite it as an **estimand**: what number would answer it? Is
it a question about **seeing** or about **doing**? *(Week 3)*

**A3.** *Concept vs. variable.* A headline talks about a **concept**. The data contain a
**variable**.

a. Give three different variables someone could use to measure "education" in Nepal.
   Could they give different answers to the same question?
b. The World Bank variable "women's college enrollment (% gross)" can be more than 100%.
   How is that possible? What does that tell you about reading variable names?
c. Why is a **proxy** like a **descendant** in a DAG? *(Week 4)*

**A4.** *What decided who got X?* For each study, name the design (randomized
experiment, natural experiment, before/after with a comparison group, or
cross-sectional comparison). Then say what decided who got the program.

a. A municipality had 400 applicants for 200 places in a free coding course, and chose
   who got in by lottery. Researchers compare the winners and losers a year later.
b. An NGO compares child health in districts that have its clinics with districts that
   don't, using one year of survey data.
c. Twenty schools started a new maths curriculum in 2023. Twenty similar schools
   started it in 2025. Researchers compare how scores changed from 2022 to 2024 in both
   groups.
d. For each of 60 wards, researchers flipped a coin to decide which wards got new
   water filters.

Which design has the most back doors to worry about? Why?

**A5.** *"After controlling for…"* Each sentence comes from the methods section of a
study. Is the control variable a **fork**, a **pipe** (mediator), or a **collider**? Was
it a good idea to control for it (or select on it)?

a. "Clinic visits were linked to better child health, after controlling for household
   wealth."
b. "The fertilizer subsidy raised rice yields. But after controlling for how much
   fertilizer each farmer used, the effect disappeared."
c. "Among students who passed the SEE, those from richer families studied fewer hours."

**A6.** *Who is it about?* Countries with higher internet use have a lower share of
young people who are not in school, work, or training.

a. Can you conclude that a young person in Nepal who starts using the internet is less
   likely to end up out of school and work? Why or why not?
b. What is the name for this mistake?
c. Give one way the country-level pattern could be true even if internet use made
   no difference to any individual.

**A7.** True or false? Give a one-sentence reason for each.

a. If a program's effect is "not significant," the program did nothing.
b. The stars (\*, \*\*, \*\*\*) in a table tell you how big an effect is.
c. A well-run randomized experiment in Bihar tells us what would happen in Madhesh.
d. A program that raises the *average* score can still make some students worse off.
e. A small study that finds a large, surprising effect deserves more doubt than a large
   study that finds a small, expected one.
f. If a risk "halves," the absolute change must be large.

# Part B: Critique a study

Read this study summary. **It is made up.** The program, the NGO, and the numbers do
not exist.

::: {.callout-note title="Fictional study: TabletLearn"}
**Headline:** *"Tablets boost learning: pass rates up 10%."*

The NGO TabletLearn gave every grade 9 student a tablet with maths and science lessons
in 30 private schools in Kathmandu Valley. Schools **applied** to join. After one year,
the NGO compared these 30 schools with 30 schools that did not apply.

- **Outcome:** a practice exam written by the NGO. 66% of students in tablet schools
  passed, compared with 60% in the other schools.
- The NGO says it measured **10 outcomes** in total (attendance, homework completion,
  several subject scores, and so on). The report shows the practice-exam result.
- Only schools where the tablets **still worked at the end of the year** were included.
  Five schools whose tablets broke were dropped.
- The program cost **Rs 12,000 per student**.
- The report includes this table. The outcome is the practice-exam score, in points.

| | Estimate | Std. error | |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| Tablet program | 4.0 | 1.5 | \*\* |
| Student attendance (days) | 0.30 | 0.05 | \*\*\* |
| Household income (log) | 2.5 | 0.8 | \*\* |
| Distance to school (km) | −0.40 | 0.30 | |

The NGO concludes: *"Every public school in Nepal should get tablets."*
:::

Answer one question at a time.

**B1.** *What exactly is the claim?* Is the headline descriptive, predictive, or causal?
Which word tells you? Write the estimand the NGO *seems* to have in mind.

**B2.** *What did they actually measure?* The headline says "learning." What was
measured? Give one reason the NGO's own practice exam might not match "learning."

**B3.** *How was the data made?* What decided which schools got tablets? Draw a DAG with
the tablet program, the exam score, and at least one unmeasured cause of both. Name the
structure.

**B4.** *What's in their DAG, and what's in their model?*

a. The model "controls for" student attendance. Draw an arrow from the tablet program to
   attendance, if you think it belongs. Is attendance a fork, a pipe, or a collider? What
   does controlling for it do to the program's estimate?
b. Only schools with working tablets were included. Tablets might keep working in
   well-run schools, and well-run schools might also have better exam results. What
   structure is this? Which way might it push the result?

**B5.** *Who is it about?* Who was studied? Who is the NGO's conclusion about? List
two differences between the two groups that could change the effect.

**B6.** *How big?*

a. The headline says pass rates rose "10%." What was the change in **percentage
   points**? Show how both numbers come from 60% and 66%.
b. In a school of 1,000 grade 9 students, how many extra students would pass?
c. Using the cost of Rs 12,000 per student, about how much does each *extra* passing
   student cost? (Assume, for now, that the 6-point gap is all caused by the tablets.)

**B7.** *How sure?* Use the table.

a. Write the rough plausible range (estimate ± 2 × std. error) for the tablet program
   and for distance to school.
b. Distance to school has no stars. Does that mean distance doesn't matter? Explain.

**B8.** *How plausible was it before?* *(Week 1)*

a. Suppose that before seeing this study, you think only 1 in 10 programs like this
   truly raise exam scores. Studies like this have about 50% power, and use α = 0.05.
   What is P( true effect | significant result )?
b. ★ The NGO measured 10 outcomes. Suppose the tablets did nothing for any of them, and
   each outcome has a 5% chance of a false "significant" result, independently. What is
   the chance that **at least one** of the 10 looks significant anyway?

**B9.** Which of the seven questions was hardest to answer from what the NGO reported?
What is the **one thing** you'd need to know before acting?

# Part C: Worked case, bicycles for girls

The lecture discussed Muralidharan & Prakash (2017), *Cycling to School*. From the
slides: Bihar gave girls entering secondary school money for a bicycle, starting in
2006. The finding was that girls' secondary enrollment rose substantially and the gender
gap narrowed. The design was a **triple difference**: girls vs. boys, Bihar vs.
Jharkhand, before vs. after. Use only this information; you don't need the paper.

**C1.** *Claim.* Is the finding descriptive, predictive, or causal? Write it as an
estimand using the template from Part 2 of the lecture.

**C2.** *Design.* Explain in plain words why each comparison is there.

a. Why not just compare girls in Bihar **before vs. after** 2006?
b. Why also compare girls with **boys** in Bihar?
c. Why also compare with **Jharkhand**?
d. What has to be true for this design to work? Finish the sentence: *"Without the
   program, the gap between girls and boys in Bihar would have changed…"*

**C3.** ★ *A triple difference by hand.* These numbers are **invented** for practice and
are **not** from the paper. They are the share (%) of children enrolled in secondary
school.

| | Before | After |
|---|---:|---:|
| Bihar girls | 30 | 45 |
| Bihar boys | 50 | 58 |
| Jharkhand girls | 32 | 40 |
| Jharkhand boys | 52 | 58 |

a. How much did enrollment change for Bihar girls? Is that the effect of the program?
b. Subtract the change for Bihar boys. What do you get?
c. Do the same for Jharkhand (girls' change minus boys' change).
d. Subtract (c) from (b). This is the triple difference. Compare the three answers in
   (a), (b) and (d). Why do they shrink?

**C4.** *DAG.* Draw a DAG for how the program could raise enrollment. Include at least
the program, owning a bicycle, travel time or safety on the way to school, and
enrollment. A later study "controls for whether the girl owns a bicycle." What happens
to the estimated effect of the program, and why?

**C5.** *Who.* Should Madhesh Province copy the program? List three ways Madhesh might
differ from Bihar in 2006 that could make the effect bigger or smaller. Which girls
would probably gain the **least** from a bicycle?

**C6.** *Size and certainty.* Before funding it in Madhesh, what would you want the
effect stated in? Give the units, and name one **alternative** you'd compare it to.

**C7.** *Prior plausibility.* Was this a surprising, cheap, convenient finding, or a
plausible one with a clear mechanism? How should that affect how much you trust it?

**C8.** *Vote again.* Would you fund it in Madhesh? Answer yes, no, or "not yet," and
name the one thing you would need to know first.

# Part D: From a decision to an estimand

**D1.** For each situation, fill in: *"If the answer is high, I'll \_\_\_. If it's
low, I'll \_\_\_."* Then say whether the analysis is worth doing.

a. A ward office has already spent its budget building a footbridge. It now wants a
   study on whether the bridge raises school attendance.
b. A savings cooperative is deciding whether to offer lower interest rates to women's
   groups. It wants to know if lower rates lead to more repaid loans.
c. A school is deciding whether to start a free morning tiffin for grades 1–3.

**D2.** Which of these are real questions (ones that could change a decision)? Rewrite
the ones that aren't.

a. "What do the data say about migration?"
b. "Should Pokhara subsidize bus passes for grade 11–12 students next year?"
c. "Is women's education important?"
d. "Should our district hire 20 more health workers or build 2 more health posts?"

**D3.** A municipality asks: *"Should we pay for free school meals for grades 1–5?"*
Fill in the estimand template:

| Piece | Your answer |
|---|---|
| Population | |
| Outcome | |
| Intervention | |
| Compared to what | |
| Time | |
| Summary | |

Then write the whole estimand as one sentence: *"Among \[population\], what is the
\[summary\] of \[outcome\] after \[time\], if \[intervention\] compared to
\[alternative\]?"*

**D4.** Each estimand below is missing something. Name the missing piece(s) and fix it.

a. "The effect of microfinance on women's income."
b. "Among rice farmers in Chitwan, the difference in average yield if they get
   drought-resistant seed."
c. "The effect of the bicycle program compared to a cash transfer of the same value."

**D5.** *Compared to what?* For the bicycle program, compare two estimands: (i) bicycle
vs. **no program**, and (ii) bicycle vs. **a cash transfer of the same value**. Could
they give different answers? Which one matters if the municipality has already
decided to spend the money on girls' schooling somehow?

**D6.** ★ *Is it worth finding out?* A bicycle costs Rs 10,000 per girl. The council will
only fund the program if each **extra** girl enrolled costs **Rs 200,000 or less**.

a. What is the smallest effect, in percentage points, at which the program is worth
   it? *(Hint: if the program raises enrollment by e percentage points, 100 bicycles
   produce e extra enrolled girls.)*
b. For a 4-point effect, how much does each extra enrolled girl cost?
c. Three studies give these plausible ranges for the effect. For each, what should the
   council do?
   - (i) 8 to 15 points
   - (ii) −1 to 3 points
   - (iii) 2 to 12 points
d. For case (iii), why might a **small pilot, designed as an experiment,** be the best
   decision?

# Part E: The target trial

**E1.** Use your estimand from D3 (school meals). If you could run **any** experiment,
what would it be? Answer: who would you randomize, to what, and when would you measure
the outcome? Why is a coin flip so useful here? *(Hint: what does it do to the arrows
into the program?)*

**E2.** Now suppose this is the data you **actually** have (also made up): one
household survey from 2023. For each household, it records whether a daughter aged
15–16 is enrolled in school, whether the household owns a bicycle, the distance to the
nearest secondary school, and household income.

You want to know whether giving girls bicycles would raise enrollment. Fill in the
table with at least three rows.

| Ideal experiment | Data we have | Gap |
|---|---|---|
| | | |
| | | |
| | | |

Which variables would you need to measure to close the back doors? Which could you
measure, and which not?

**E3.** The lecture said to name your limitations **before** you see the results. Why
does the order matter?

**E4.** ★ Write the target trial for the Bihar study (Part C). Then compare it with what
the researchers could actually do. What is the biggest gap, and how did the triple
difference try to get around it?

# Part F: Applied

**F1.** *Your project.* Open your project page in `projects/`.

a. Rewrite your project's question using the **estimand template**.
b. What is your **target trial**? Be concrete: what would be randomized, and among
   whom? (It is fine if this experiment is impossible. Say why.)
c. Fill in the "Ideal experiment / Data we have / Gap" table for your project. The data
   you have is World Bank 2022.
d. List your **scope limits**:
   - One year, cross-sectional. What can't one snapshot tell you?
   - Country-level. What can your project say about individual people or households?
   - Measurement. Pick one of your variables. Does it mean what its label says?
e. Which of the seven questions would a skeptic ask you **first**? Write a short answer
   to it.

**F2.** *A one-page critique memo.* This is the main assignment for the week. Pick a
real report or finding from your own work: a government report, an NGO evaluation, a
news story, a consultant's slide deck.

- Organize the memo by the **seven questions**: one short paragraph each.
- End with a section called **"What I'd need to see before acting on this."**
- Keep it to one page. Short and clear beats long and complete.

Here is a short example, written about a **made-up** claim, to show the shape:

::: {.callout-tip title="Example memo (fictional claim)" collapse="true"}
**Claim:** *"Wards with more health posts have fewer child deaths, so every ward should
get a second health post."*

1. **Claim.** Causal ("so every ward should get"), but the evidence is a comparison
   between wards.
2. **Measured.** "Child deaths" is deaths *recorded* at the ward office. Wards with more
   health posts may record deaths more completely, which would hide part of the effect.
3. **Design.** Cross-sectional. Health posts were placed by the government, probably in
   richer or better-connected wards. People didn't get a health post by coin flip.
4. **DAG.** Wealth and road access are forks (they cause both health posts and child
   survival). The report doesn't control for either.
5. **Who.** Wards in one district. The claim is about every ward in the country.
6. **Size and certainty.** The report says "fewer deaths" but gives no number or range.
7. **Prior.** It is plausible that health posts help. The open question is *how much*,
   and whether a second post adds as much as the first.

**What I'd need to see before acting on this:** the comparison repeated within wards of
similar wealth and road access, the effect stated per 1,000 children with a range, and
the cost of a second health post next to the alternatives.
:::

# Part G: R challenge (optional)

**G1.** Write an R function `plausible_range(estimate, se)` that returns the low and high
ends of estimate ± 2 × std. error, and whether the range crosses zero. Use it to check
your answers to B7 for all four rows of the TabletLearn table.

**G2.** ★ *Self-selection, simulated.* Simulate 1,000 schools. Each school has a
`motivation` drawn from `rnorm()`. Motivated schools are more likely to join the
tablet program: `tablet <- rbinom(n, 1, plogis(2 * motivation))`. The exam score is
`50 + 5 * motivation + effect * tablet + rnorm(n, 0, 5)`.

a. Set `effect <- 0` (the tablets do nothing). Compute the average score of tablet
   schools minus the average score of other schools. Repeat this 200 times and take the
   average. What do you get, and why isn't it 0?
b. Now give out tablets by coin flip instead: `tablet <- rbinom(n, 1, 0.5)`. What is
   the difference now?
c. Repeat (a) and (b) with `effect <- 3`. Which design recovers the true effect?
d. Connect this to question 3 of the seven: *"What decided who got X?"*

# Part H: Reflection

**H1.** At the start of the lecture you were asked whether you'd fund a program based on
one confident headline. In a short paragraph:

- Did your answer change by the end? Why?
- Which of the seven questions do you now think is the most often skipped, in the
  reports you see at work?
- Name one thing you used to believe from a single study or news story that you would
  now want to check.
